taxonomy.note: Kew accepts Yucca rupicola; native range is south-central Texas (southeastern Edwards Plateau) to northeastern Mexico. FNA describes it as endemic to the southeastern Edwards Plateau within its U.S. range.

evidence: Hays — UT Plant Resources Center Flora of Purola Preserve lists Yucca rupicola among naturally occurring, non-introduced plants of northern Hays County.
Travis — Balcones Canyonlands Preserve plant list for Travis County includes twist-leaf yucca (Yucca rupicola).
Williamson — UT Plant Resources Center provides a detailed Vascular Plants of Williamson County treatment for Yucca rupicola.
target_zone_range.guardrail: County decision uses explicit county/local records alongside BONAP/NPSOT/Kew range context. No county is inferred from ecoregion membership alone.

morphology.look_here_first: Look at the leaves before the flower: a low, essentially trunkless colony with flexible dark-green leaves that twist helically and have wavy/denticulate orange to reddish-brown margins.
diagnostic_traits: flexible lanceolate leaves, 35–60 cm long and 1.7–4 cm wide
leaves conspicuously twisted and strongly concave
leaf margins wavy or minutely toothed, dark orange to reddish brown
inflorescence rises well beyond the rosette
fruit erect, dry, dehiscent capsule rather than a fleshy berry

confusers.separator: Both are low colony-forming yuccas, but Y. rupicola has broader flexible twisted leaves with orange/red wavy-toothed margins; Y. constricta has much narrower mostly straight leaves with whitish filiferous margins and a deeply waist-constricted capsule.
Pale yucca is usually glaucous blue-green with straighter leaves and flatter yellowish margins; Y. rupicola is darker green, visibly twisted, and has wavy orange/red margins.
